impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting JMOL that claims directed to methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity, reinstating a jury verdict that Lilly willfully infringed Teva's headache patents covering the use of humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies to treat headache. The case involves blockbuster migraine drugs (Teva's Ajovy and Lilly's competing product) and has major implications for how courts evaluate written description and enablement for antibody-based method-of-treatment claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biopharmaceutical innovators holding method-of-treatment claims involving antibody therapeutics, reinforcing that genus claims may satisfy § 112 requirements when the specification discloses known methods and representative species.
impacts.negativeImplications: Creates greater exposure for companies developing competing biologics, as broadly drafted antibody method-of-treatment claims may be harder to invalidate on written-description or enablement grounds.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing emulated function calls to a model are abstract under step one of the Alice framework, and whether damages based on foreign sales of cybersecurity software were properly awarded.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated a $185 million jury verdict, holding that Columbia's cybersecurity patents were directed to abstract ideas at Alice step one and remanding for step two analysis. The court also held that damages based on Norton's foreign software sales were improperly awarded, reinforcing limits on extraterritorial patent damages. The court further vacated enhanced damages and attorneys' fees tied to an improper contempt finding.
impacts.positiveImplications: Benefits technology companies defending against patent assertions by reinforcing Alice eligibility scrutiny for software-implemented detection methods and limiting extraterritorial damages exposure for global software sales.
impacts.negativeImplications: Universities and patent holders asserting cybersecurity and software patents face heightened eligibility risk, and the ruling constrains damages models that include foreign revenue streams.

impacts.caseName: VLSI Technology LLC v. Intel Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly granted summary judgment of noninfringement of a multicore processor patent based on extraterritoriality and rejection of the doctrine of equivalents theory, and whether it properly struck certain damages expert theories.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed in part the district court's grant of summary judgment to Intel on VLSI's multicore processor patent, finding genuine issues of material fact remained. The court addressed the scope of extraterritoriality limits on method claims where steps occur partly abroad and affirmed the striking of certain damages theories for inadequate disclosure. This is part of the high-profile VLSI v. Intel patent litigation involving billions in potential exposure.
impacts.positiveImplications: Clarifies for patent holders that extraterritoriality defenses may not automatically defeat infringement claims for method patents where significant steps occur domestically, preserving litigation options against major semiconductor companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies face continued exposure to large damages claims from patent assertion entities, and the ruling may complicate summary judgment strategies based on extraterritoriality for globally deployed technology.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether genuine disputes of material fact precluded summary judgment on inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims related to patents obtained despite the existence of prior art (CYMAX) known to the applicants.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgments on both inequitable conduct (which had been granted for Global Tubing) and Walker Process fraud (which had been granted for Tenaris), finding genuine factual disputes on both issues. The case involves allegations that Tenaris obtained coiled tubing patents while concealing its knowledge of prior art from acquired company assets, potentially rendering the patents unenforceable and exposing Tenaris to antitrust liability.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies acquiring prior art through asset purchases are reminded that courts will scrutinize whether known prior art was disclosed during patent prosecution; competitors have viable pathways to challenge patents obtained through alleged inequitable conduct.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire businesses and subsequently patent similar technology face significant litigation risk, including potential Walker Process antitrust liability, when prior art from the acquired entity was not disclosed to the PTO.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether there was a legally sufficient evidentiary basis for the jury's finding that asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed trade secret misappropriation liability findings, holding that the plaintiff failed to show its asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying information was generally known. The court also reversed on patent inventorship, reasoning that contributions of generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting claim was affirmed. The ruling vacated a reasonable royalty, exemplary damages, and a permanent injunction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens defenses against trade secret claims by requiring plaintiffs to clearly establish that asserted secrets are not generally known in the industry, raising the evidentiary bar for trade secret protection.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on trade secret protection for medical device designs and processes face greater risk of having claims rejected where the underlying concepts are shown to be generally known, even if specific implementations differ.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, distinguishing between claims directed to abstract mathematical optimization and claims tied to specific hardware implementations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated eligibility for certain patent claims directed to non-uniform constellation designs (used in broadcast communications like ATSC 3.0), finding them abstract, while affirming eligibility for claims tied to specific transmitter and receiver apparatus implementations. The ruling draws an important line between abstract mathematical optimization and patent-eligible applied technology in the communications standards space.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies implementing communications standards may benefit from narrowed patent exposure where asserted claims are directed to abstract mathematical relationships rather than specific hardware implementations.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the communications and signal processing space face heightened eligibility risk for claims framed around optimized mathematical mappings, even where those mappings have been incorporated into industry standards.

impacts.caseName: Apple Inc. v. International Trade Commission
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC properly found that Apple Watch models incorporating blood oxygen measurement functionality infringed Masimo's patents covering user-worn physiological measurement devices, and whether Masimo established a domestic industry.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches infringing Masimo's blood oxygen measurement patents, upholding the limited exclusion order barring importation. The court found no error in the ITC's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, or infringement findings. This ruling sustains a significant import ban affecting one of Apple's flagship products.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates the ITC as an effective enforcement venue for medical technology patent holders against major consumer electronics companies, reinforcing that even incremental features in mass-market devices can trigger import exclusion.
impacts.negativeImplications: Major consumer electronics companies face significant supply chain and product design disruption when ITC exclusion orders are upheld, particularly for features integrated into flagship products with global distribution.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify beyond personal knowledge at summary judgment, and whether the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b) requires that the prior art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that 30(b)(6) testimony is admissible at summary judgment even when the witness lacks personal knowledge of the events, and that the on-sale bar does not require sales to expressly disclose a device's internal functionality. The court also addressed the admissibility of source code as non-hearsay evidence.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens invalidity defenses by confirming that the on-sale bar applies based on commercial sales of devices embodying claimed technology, regardless of whether the sale expressly disclosed internal functionality, and that corporate representative testimony is broadly admissible.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face increased vulnerability to on-sale bar challenges where prior commercial products embodied claimed technology, even if the relevant functionality was not publicly disclosed or advertised at the time of sale.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the Board on exercising discretion to deny IPR institution constitute a 'general statement of policy' exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under APA § 553(b).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's instructions governing discretionary denial of IPR institution are general policy statements exempt from APA notice-and-comment rulemaking requirements. The court emphasized that Congress provided no legal right to IPR institution and that the Director retains ultimate non-institution authority, insulated from judicial review. This forecloses a significant procedural challenge to PTO discretionary denial practices.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the PTO's continued broad discretion to deny institution of IPR proceedings, particularly where parallel litigation exists, without the constraints that formal rulemaking would impose.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patents through IPR face continued uncertainty from discretionary denials guided by internal PTO policies that are not subject to public notice-and-comment or judicial review on substantive grounds.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board correctly construed the claim term 'encryption information' in a patent covering partly encrypted media streaming systems, and whether Netflix's obviousness challenge should have prevailed under the correct construction.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Board's claim construction of 'encryption information' in DivX's streaming media patent, vacated the Board's decision rejecting Netflix's obviousness challenge, and remanded for further proceedings. The case has significant implications for the streaming industry's use of adaptive bitrate streaming with partial encryption, a technology deployed across major platforms.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming technology companies benefit from the narrower claim construction, potentially reducing exposure to infringement claims covering widely used adaptive bitrate streaming and partial encryption techniques.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the digital media streaming space may face weakened claims if broadly construed encryption-related terms are narrowed on appeal, reducing the scope of enforceable patent rights.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a damages expert report and granting summary judgment based on absence of a remedy in a patent infringement case involving virtual network optimization technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft, finding that the district court applied too stringent a standard in excluding the expert's opinions on damages related to Microsoft's Azure SmartNIC and VFP technology. The ruling reinforces that patent plaintiffs must be given reasonable opportunity to present damages evidence and that expert exclusion should not be used to effectively adjudicate the merits.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders, particularly smaller entities suing large technology companies, benefit from the ruling's protection against overly aggressive expert exclusion that would effectively eliminate their ability to pursue remedies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Large technology companies may face greater difficulty obtaining early dispositive rulings through Daubert motions targeting damages experts, potentially prolonging patent litigation to trial.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an ITC respondent that missed the deadline for a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) may obtain such a stay by dismissing and refiling its declaratory judgment action.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that an ITC respondent cannot circumvent the statutory deadline for seeking a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action by dismissing and refiling the declaratory judgment complaint. The ruling closes a potential procedural loophole in the coordination between ITC and district court patent proceedings, with direct implications for pharmaceutical patent litigation strategy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders bringing ITC actions benefit from certainty that respondents cannot manipulate mandatory stay deadlines through tactical refiling, ensuring parallel district court proceedings continue on schedule.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC respondents and generic/biosimilar drug developers lose a potential strategic tool for delaying district court patent proceedings by refiling declaratory judgment actions to reset mandatory stay deadlines.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users, including approval of attorneys' fees, costs, and incentive awards to class representatives.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by using PACER fees to fund non-PACER expenses. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to nonprofit class representatives, noting that hundreds of thousands of PACER users will be fully or substantially reimbursed for fees paid during the eight-year class period.
impacts.positiveImplications: Validates the use of class action settlements to recover overcharges from government systems, providing a model for future challenges to government fee-setting practices that exceed statutory authority.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in its obviousness determination regarding sensor-based logistics patents, and whether a non-party to district court litigation can file an IPR petition on the same patents on the filing deadline of the actual defendant.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness finding regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded, while declining to review the Board's denial of FedEx's motion to terminate the IPR. The case raises significant questions about the practice of third parties filing IPR petitions on behalf of or in coordination with time-barred parties, a tactic with growing implications for patent litigation strategy.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders may benefit from the vacatur of the obviousness finding and the continued scrutiny of third-party IPR filings that appear coordinated with time-barred litigation defendants.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR petitions as a defensive strategy face uncertainty, as courts increasingly scrutinize whether such filings are improperly coordinated to circumvent the one-year time bar.

impacts.caseName: Willis Electric Co., Ltd. v. Polygroup Ltd. (Macao Commercial Offshore)
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board erred in finding the challenged patent claims obvious, and whether the jury's damages award was supported by sufficient evidence in a case involving pre-lit artificial tree technology.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the denial of Polygroup's JMOL of obviousness and motion for new trial on damages, upholding a jury verdict of patent infringement covering pre-lit artificial tree technology with integrated electrical connections. The ruling sustains Willis's patent protection in a commercially significant consumer products market and validates the jury's damages methodology.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in consumer products markets benefit from the affirmance of jury verdicts on both validity and damages, demonstrating that mechanical innovation patents can withstand obviousness challenges even in seemingly simple technology areas.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors in the seasonal consumer products industry face continued patent enforcement risk and validated damages models for products incorporating patented integrated connection features.
